items.p: of new bonds sold in fiscal 2025 to pay for schools, jails, roads and other construction, not counting $7 billion sold to refinance older debt. Most are general obligation bonds, backed by the property tax, or bonds of the Transitional Finance Authority, a borrowing agency the state created for the city that is backed by the income tax. The water system borrows separately. What the bonds build is not in the squares; the yearly interest and principal are, as debt service.

items.p: of bonds and notes outstanding at the end of fiscal 2025, mostly general obligation and Transitional Finance Authority bonds. Counting long-term leases and other obligations too, the Comptroller puts the city's debt at $134 billion, or $15,763 a resident.

items.p: is the shortfall the city's own financial plan projects for fiscal 2028, growing to $8.5 billion by 2030. The Comptroller's estimates differ: $7.3 billion in 2028, easing to $6.8 billion in 2030, plus a $743 million shortfall that could open this year. Each budget must balance before it is adopted, so these are the amounts future budgets will have to close.

note: Also beside the budget: the New York City Water Board, which bills for water and sewer service and pays the city for running the system ($2.4 billion in fiscal 2027); NYC Health + Hospitals and the New York City Housing Authority, separate public corporations that keep their own books and receive city money that appears in the squares; and the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), a state authority whose city payments, about $1.7 billion, also appear in the squares.
